findings.title: Async legacy writes are cancelled with the request
findings.body: Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine using context.WithTimeoutCause on the incoming request context. That child is cancelled as soon as the parent request context is cancelled, which the apiserver does when the handler returns—before the 10s timeout can matter. The legacy write that mode 3 relies on as a safety copy therefore fails with context.Canceled (or never runs to completion), so legacy storage diverges from unified storage while the API still returns success. The goroutines also drop the legacy error instead of logging it, so the failure is silent. Detach from cancellation (for example context.WithoutCancel) before applying the timeout, and log legacy failures.

findings.title: Legacy update no longer applies the same object snapshot
findings.body: Update now passes the original objInfo into both Storage.Update and the async Legacy.Update. The previous implementation resolved UpdatedObject once and wrapped that snapshot so both stores wrote the same object. UpdatedObjectInfo is often single-use or not concurrency-safe (patch/apply transformers mutate state and are applied against each store's own current object). Calling it again from the goroutine, concurrently with the in-flight request, can write a different object to legacy, double-apply a patch, or panic. Snapshot the object produced by the unified update and give legacy a fixed UpdatedObjectInfo.

findings.title: Legacy create receives the object mutated by unified create
findings.body: After Storage.Create returns, the same obj pointer is passed to the async Legacy.Create. Unified/etcd create fills in resourceVersion, UID, and timestamps on that object. Kubernetes create requires an empty resourceVersion, so the legacy create will be rejected or persist unified-storage metadata. Copy the object before the storage create (or deep-copy the pre-create input for legacy) so the safety write is a real create of the client's object.

findings.title: Dual-writer metrics record the wrong store or label
findings.body: On Storage.Create failure the duration is recorded with recordLegacyDuration (line 45); Storage.Update failure does the same (line 129). Delete success records recordStorageDuration with the object name as the kind label (line 106) instead of options.Kind. DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records recordStorageDuration (line 166) instead of recordLegacyDuration. Failure and latency dashboards for mode 3 will attribute unified-storage errors to legacy, legacy delete-collection latency to storage, and delete metrics to a per-object series, so the safety-write signal this mode depends on is wrong.

findings.title: Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy goroutines
findings.body: Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately while Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection may still be running legacy writes in unbounded goroutines. Shutdown or mode switches can destroy a store underneath those calls, dropping the safety write or racing use-after-close. Track the goroutines and wait for them (with the existing timeout) before Destroy returns.

findings.title: Mode 3 playlist tests assume synchronous legacy writes
findings.body: The new mode 3 integration cases reuse doPlaylistTests, which immediately lists and gets playlists through the legacy /api/playlists endpoints after k8s create, update, and delete (around the legacy search at line 522 and getFromBothAPIs). Mode 3 returns as soon as unified storage succeeds and only then writes legacy in the background, and that background context is cancelled when the request ends. Those assertions will flake or fail, and they never wait for the legacy write. The unit tests in dualwriter_mode3_test.go have the same gap: they return without waiting for or asserting the legacy mock calls, so a missing or cancelled legacy write still passes.
